claim: In populations of African ancestry, two apolipoprotein-L1 (APOL1) variants with a recessive kidney disease risk, named G1 and G2, occur at high frequency.
source: In populations of African ancestry, two apolipoprotein-L1 (APOL1) variants with a recessive kidney disease risk, named G1 and G2, occur at high frequency.
evidence: This is established knowledge about APOL1 variants in African populations, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: APOL1 is a trypanolytic protein that confers innate resistance to most African trypanosomes.
source: APOL1 is a trypanolytic protein that confers innate resistance to most African trypanosomes, but not Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense or T.b. gambiense, which cause human African trypanosomiasis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about APOL1 function, referenced in the introduction.

claim: APOL1 does not confer innate resistance to Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense or T.b. gambiense.
source: APOL1 is a trypanolytic protein that confers innate resistance to most African trypanosomes, but not Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense or T.b. gambiense, which cause human African trypanosomiasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about APOL1's lack of activity against human-infective trypanosomes.

claim: T.b. rhodesiense and T.b. gambiense cause human African trypanosomiasis.
source: APOL1 is a trypanolytic protein that confers innate resistance to most African trypanosomes, but not Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense or T.b. gambiense, which cause human African trypanosomiasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the causative agents of HAT.

claim: G2 demonstrates a five-fold dominant protective association against T.b. rhodesiense infection.
source: We demonstrate a five-fold dominant protective association for G2 against T.b. rhodesiense infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: G2 associates with faster progression of T.b. gambiense trypanosomiasis.
source: G2 associates with faster progression of T.b. gambiense trypanosomiasis, while G1 associates with asymptomatic carriage and undetectable parasitemia.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: G1 associates with asymptomatic carriage and undetectable parasitemia in T.b. gambiense infection.
source: G2 associates with faster progression of T.b. gambiense trypanosomiasis, while G1 associates with asymptomatic carriage and undetectable parasitemia.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: Both forms of human African trypanosomiasis are implicated in the selection and persistence of APOL1 kidney disease variants.
source: These results implicate both forms of human African trypanosomiasis in the selection and persistence of otherwise detrimental APOL1 kidney disease variants.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings about associations with both T.b. rhodesiense and T.b. gambiense.

claim: Chronic kidney disease affects millions worldwide.
source: Like sickle-cell disease, chronic kidney disease also affects millions worldwide (Global Burden of Disease Study 2013 Collaborators, 2015), with a disproportionate risk in populations of recent sub-Saharan African ancestry (National Institutes of Health and National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, 2010; Norris and Agodoa, 2002; McClellan et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Global Burden of Disease Study.

claim: Populations of recent sub-Saharan African ancestry have a disproportionate risk of chronic kidney disease.
source: Like sickle-cell disease, chronic kidney disease also affects millions worldwide (Global Burden of Disease Study 2013 Collaborators, 2015), with a disproportionate risk in populations of recent sub-Saharan African ancestry (National Institutes of Health and National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, 2010; Norris and Agodoa, 2002; McClellan et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: In African-Americans, a large component of chronic kidney disease disparity has been attributed to APOL1 G1 and G2 variants.
source: In African-Americans a large component of this disparity has been attributed to two common genetic variants of APOL1 (MIM 603743), known as G1 and G2 (Genovese et al., 2010; Tzur et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Genovese et al., 2010 and Tzur et al., 2010.

claim: G1 and G2 variants are closely spaced in the C-terminal domain of APOL1 but are located on separate haplotypes.
source: These variants are closely spaced in the C-terminal domain of APOL1 but are located on separate haplotypes (Genovese et al., 2010) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Approximately 13% of African-Americans possess a high-risk G1/G1, G2/G2 or G1/G2 genotype.
source: Individuals possessing a high-risk G1/G1, G2/G2 or G1/G2 genotype composed of two risk alleles (approximately 13% of African-Americans [Friedman et al., 2011]), are strongly predisposed to a wide spectrum of chronic kidney disorders that includes focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (Genovese et al., 2010; Kopp et al., 2011), HIV-associated nephropathy (Kopp et al., 2011; Kasembeli et al., 2015) and end-stage renal disease (Genovese et al., 2010; Tzur et al., 2010; Freedman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Friedman et al., 2011.

claim: Individuals with high-risk APOL1 genotypes are strongly predisposed to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.
source: Individuals possessing a high-risk G1/G1, G2/G2 or G1/G2 genotype composed of two risk alleles (approximately 13% of African-Americans [Friedman et al., 2011]), are strongly predisposed to a wide spectrum of chronic kidney disorders that includes focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (Genovese et al., 2010; Kopp et al., 2011), HIV-associated nephropathy (Kopp et al., 2011; Kasembeli et al., 2015) and end-stage renal disease (Genovese et al., 2010; Tzur et al., 2010; Freedman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Genovese et al., 2010 and Kopp et al., 2011.

claim: Individuals with high-risk APOL1 genotypes are strongly predisposed to HIV-associated nephropathy.
source: Individuals possessing a high-risk G1/G1, G2/G2 or G1/G2 genotype composed of two risk alleles (approximately 13% of African-Americans [Friedman et al., 2011]), are strongly predisposed to a wide spectrum of chronic kidney disorders that includes focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (Genovese et al., 2010; Kopp et al., 2011), HIV-associated nephropathy (Kopp et al., 2011; Kasembeli et al., 2015) and end-stage renal disease (Genovese et al., 2010; Tzur et al., 2010; Freedman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kopp et al., 2011 and Kasembeli et al., 2015.

claim: Individuals with high-risk APOL1 genotypes are strongly predisposed to end-stage renal disease.
source: Individuals possessing a high-risk G1/G1, G2/G2 or G1/G2 genotype composed of two risk alleles (approximately 13% of African-Americans [Friedman et al., 2011]), are strongly predisposed to a wide spectrum of chronic kidney disorders that includes focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (Genovese et al., 2010; Kopp et al., 2011), HIV-associated nephropathy (Kopp et al., 2011; Kasembeli et al., 2015) and end-stage renal disease (Genovese et al., 2010; Tzur et al., 2010; Freedman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Genovese et al., 2010, Tzur et al., 2010, and Freedman et al., 2014.

claim: APOL1 G1 and G2 are prevalent only in populations of recent African heritage.
source: APOL1 G1 and G2 are prevalent only in populations of recent African heritage (Genovese et al., 2010; Kopp et al., 2011), with evidence for a selective sweep within the last 10,000 years (Genovese et al., 2010), indicative of strong positive selection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Genovese et al., 2010 and Kopp et al., 2011.

claim: There is evidence for a selective sweep of APOL1 variants within the last 10,000 years.
source: APOL1 G1 and G2 are prevalent only in populations of recent African heritage (Genovese et al., 2010; Kopp et al., 2011), with evidence for a selective sweep within the last 10,000 years (Genovese et al., 2010), indicative of strong positive selection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Genovese et al., 2010.

claim: Human African trypanosomiasis has been proposed as the source of positive selective pressure on APOL1 variants.
source: Human African trypanosomiasis (HAT), a deadly parasitic disease endemic to sub-Saharan Africa, has been proposed as the source of this positive selective pressure (Genovese et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Genovese et al., 2010.

claim: T.b. rhodesiense is responsible for the acute East African form of HAT.
source: HAT is caused by two tsetse fly-transmitted African trypanosomes, Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense and T.b. gambiense, which are responsible for the acute East African form and more chronic West Africa form of the disease, respectively (Kennedy, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Kennedy, 2013.

claim: T.b. gambiense is responsible for the chronic West African form of HAT.
source: HAT is caused by two tsetse fly-transmitted African trypanosomes, Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense and T.b. gambiense, which are responsible for the acute East African form and more chronic West Africa form of the disease, respectively (Kennedy, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Kennedy, 2013.

claim: Both T.b. rhodesiense and T.b. gambiense have been responsible for widespread fatal epidemics in sub-Saharan Africa throughout recorded human history.
source: Both parasites have been responsible for widespread fatal epidemics in sub-Saharan Africa throughout recorded human history (Steverding, 2008) suggesting the potential to exert potent selection pressure on the human genome.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steverding, 2008.

claim: A heterozygous advantage model has been proposed for APOL1 G1 and G2 in which recessive susceptibility to chronic kidney disease is balanced by dominant resistance to HAT.
source: A heterozygous advantage model has been proposed for APOL1 G1 and G2 (Genovese et al., 2010) in which recessive susceptibility to chronic kidney disease is balanced by dominant resistance to one or both forms of human African trypanosomiasis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work, supported by citation to Genovese et al., 2010.

claim: APOL1 is a 398-amino acid protein consisting of a cleavable N-terminal signal peptide, a pore-forming domain, a membrane-addressing domain, and a serum resistance-associated (SRA)-interacting domain.
source: Human apolipoprotein-L1 (APOL1) is a 398-amino acid protein consisting of a cleavable N-terminal signal peptide, a pore-forming domain, a membrane-addressing domain, and a serum resistance-associated (SRA)-interacting domain.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: The polymorphisms that characterize the G1 and G2 renal risk variants are located in the SRA-interacting domain.
source: The polymorphisms that characterize the G1 and G2 renal risk variants are located in the SRA-interacting domain, the target site for binding of the SRA protein expressed by the human-infective T.b.rhodesiense parasite, which results in loss of APOL1 lytic function.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: The SRA-interacting domain is the target site for binding of the SRA protein expressed by T.b. rhodesiense.
source: The polymorphisms that characterize the G1 and G2 renal risk variants are located in the SRA-interacting domain, the target site for binding of the SRA protein expressed by the human-infective T.b.rhodesiense parasite, which results in loss of APOL1 lytic function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SRA-APOL1 interaction.

claim: SRA binding to APOL1 results in loss of APOL1 lytic function.
source: The polymorphisms that characterize the G1 and G2 renal risk variants are located in the SRA-interacting domain, the target site for binding of the SRA protein expressed by the human-infective T.b.rhodesiense parasite, which results in loss of APOL1 lytic function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of SRA.

claim: G1 consists of two missense SNPs rs73885319 (p.Ser342Gly) and rs60910145 (p.Ile384Met).
source: G1 consists of two missense SNPs rs73885319 (p.Ser342Gly) and rs60910145 (p.Ile384Met) while the G2 polymorphism, rs71785313 (p.Asn388_Tyr389del), is found on an alternative APOL1 haplotype, and represents an in-frame two amino acid deletion.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: The G2 polymorphism, rs71785313 (p.Asn388_Tyr389del), is found on an alternative APOL1 haplotype and represents an in-frame two amino acid deletion.
source: G1 consists of two missense SNPs rs73885319 (p.Ser342Gly) and rs60910145 (p.Ile384Met) while the G2 polymorphism, rs71785313 (p.Asn388_Tyr389del), is found on an alternative APOL1 haplotype, and represents an in-frame two amino acid deletion.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: APOL1 encodes a pore-forming serum protein that inserts into trypanosome membranes and effectively lyses Trypanosoma species that cause disease in animals.
source: Prior to the discovery of its association with kidney disease, APOL1 had already been recognised for encoding the pore-forming serum protein Apolipoprotein L1, which inserts into trypanosome membranes and effectively lyses the Trypanosoma species that cause disease in animals (Vanhamme et al., 2003; Pérez-Morga et al., 2005; Molina-Portela et al., 2005; Thomson and Finkelstein, 2015; Vanwalleghem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The two human-infective trypanosome subspecies have evolved independent mechanisms to resist APOL1-mediated lysis.
source: However, the two human-infective subspecies have evolved independent mechanisms to resist APOL1-mediated lysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome resistance mechanisms.

claim: In T.b. rhodesiense, APOL1 resistance is the result of an APOL1-binding protein.
source: In T.b. rhodesiense, this is the result of an APOL1-binding protein (Xong et al., 1998; De Greef et al., 1989) whereas for T.b. gambiense the mechanism of APOL1 resistance appears more complex and multifactorial (Capewell et al., 2013; Uzureau et al., 2013; DeJesus et al., 2013; Kieft et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xong et al., 1998 and De Greef et al., 1989.

claim: For T.b. gambiense, the mechanism of APOL1 resistance appears more complex and multifactorial.
source: In T.b. rhodesiense, this is the result of an APOL1-binding protein (Xong et al., 1998; De Greef et al., 1989) whereas for T.b. gambiense the mechanism of APOL1 resistance appears more complex and multifactorial (Capewell et al., 2013; Uzureau et al., 2013; DeJesus et al., 2013; Kieft et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Previous studies have shown that APOL1 G2 plasma is lytic to East African T.b. rhodesiense parasites in vitro.
source: Indeed, previous studies have shown that APOL1 G2 (and to a lesser extent G1) plasma is lytic to East African T.b. rhodesiense parasites in vitro (Genovese et al., 2010), but not West African T.b. gambiense (Genovese et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Genovese et al., 2010.

claim: APOL1 G1 plasma shows lesser lytic activity against T.b. rhodesiense parasites in vitro compared to G2.
source: Indeed, previous studies have shown that APOL1 G2 (and to a lesser extent G1) plasma is lytic to East African T.b. rhodesiense parasites in vitro (Genovese et al., 2010), but not West African T.b. gambiense (Genovese et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Genovese et al., 2010.

claim: APOL1 G2 and G1 plasma are not lytic to West African T.b. gambiense in vitro.
source: Indeed, previous studies have shown that APOL1 G2 (and to a lesser extent G1) plasma is lytic to East African T.b. rhodesiense parasites in vitro (Genovese et al., 2010), but not West African T.b. gambiense (Genovese et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Genovese et al., 2010.

claim: T.b. rhodesiense is considered the most likely candidate for positive selection of both APOL1 variants in African populations.
source: Consequently, T.b. rhodesiense is considered the most likely candidate for positive selection of both APOL1 variants in African populations (Genovese et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work, supported by citation to Genovese et al., 2010.

claim: The G1 variant appears significantly less effective at killing T.b. rhodesiense.
source: Notably, however, the G1 variant appears significantly less effective at killing T.b. rhodesiense, and is found at very high frequency in West Africa (Genovese et al., 2010; Kopp et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2013; Thomson et al., 2014), where only T.b. gambiense is endemic (Simarro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: G1 is found at very high frequency in West Africa.
source: Notably, however, the G1 variant appears significantly less effective at killing T.b. rhodesiense, and is found at very high frequency in West Africa (Genovese et al., 2010; Kopp et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2013; Thomson et al., 2014), where only T.b. gambiense is endemic (Simarro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Only T.b. gambiense is endemic in West Africa.
source: Notably, however, the G1 variant appears significantly less effective at killing T.b. rhodesiense, and is found at very high frequency in West Africa (Genovese et al., 2010; Kopp et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2013; Thomson et al., 2014), where only T.b. gambiense is endemic (Simarro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Simarro et al., 2010.

claim: A class of asymptomatic individuals has been recently identified in T.b. gambiense disease foci who exhibit a long-term T.b. gambiense-specific serological response but low or undetectable parasitemia.
source: Furthermore, a class of asymptomatic individuals has been recently identified in T.b. gambiense disease foci, who exhibit a long-term T.b. gambiense-specific serological response but low or undetectable parasitemia indicative of a latent asymptomatic infection (Koffi et al., 2006; Jamonneau et al., 2012; Bucheton et al., 2011; Ilboudo et al., 2011; Jamonneau et al., 2010; Garcia et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Parasites from asymptomatic T.b. gambiense carriers appear genetically indistinguishable from those of clinical cases.
source: Parasites from such individuals appear genetically indistinguishable from those of T.b. gambiense clinical cases (Kaboré et al., 2011), suggesting disease outcome may be mediated by, as yet unidentified, host genetic factors.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kaboré et al., 2011.

claim: Disease outcome in T.b. gambiense infection may be mediated by unidentified host genetic factors.
source: Parasites from such individuals appear genetically indistinguishable from those of T.b. gambiense clinical cases (Kaboré et al., 2011), suggesting disease outcome may be mediated by, as yet unidentified, host genetic factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic similarity of parasites from different disease outcomes.

claim: 180 controls and 184 clinically confirmed T.b. rhodesiense patients from central-eastern Uganda were genotyped for G1 and G2 polymorphisms.
source: To test the heterozygous advantage hypothesis proposed for these APOL1 variants against T.b. rhodesiense infection (Genovese et al., 2010), 180 controls and 184 clinically confirmed T.b. rhodesiense patients from a principle disease focus in central-eastern Uganda were genotyped for G1 and G2 polymorphisms.
evidence: This describes the study design and sample collection.

claim: The G1 haplotype comprises two non-synonymous substitutions, rs73885319 and rs60910145, situated just 128 bp apart and in near-perfect linkage disequilibrium.
source: The G1 haplotype comprises of two non-synonymous substitutions, rs73885319 and rs60910145 situated just 128 bp apart and in near-perfect linkage disequilibrium (Genovese et al., 2010; Kopp et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Genovese et al., 2010 and Kopp et al., 2011.

claim: A small number of individuals were identified with only a partial G1 haplotype and were excluded from the G1 haplotype association analysis.
source: In this study, as reported by others (Kopp et al., 2011; Behar et al., 2011), a small number of individuals were identified with only a partial G1 haplotype (the kidney disease risk genotype at one of the G1 polymorphism positions but the non-risk genotype at the other) and were excluded from the G1 haplotype association analysis.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision in the study.

claim: No association was found between the G1 haplotype and T.b. rhodesiense infection (p=0.50).
source: Comparing genotype frequencies in confirmed T.b. rhodesiense-infected individuals with uninfected controls found no association between the G1 haplotype and T.b. rhodesiense infection (p=0.50; Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's statistical analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: A significant dominant protective association was observed for the G2 variant against T.b. rhodesiense infection, with an odds ratio of 0.20 (95% CI: 0.07 to 0.48, p=0.0001).
source: In contrast, we observed a significant dominant protective association for the G2 variant, with an odds ratio of 0.20 (95% CI: 0.07 to 0.48, p=0.0001; Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's statistical analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: The G2 variant indicates a five-fold reduced susceptibility to T.b. rhodesiense infection for individuals that possess a single copy.
source: This indicates a five-fold reduced susceptibility to T.b. rhodesiense infection for individuals that possess a single copy of the G2 variant, compatible with a model of heterozygous protection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the odds ratio from the statistical analysis.

claim: 227 T.b. gambiense-infected individuals and 104 controls from the mangrove focus in Guinea were genotyped for G1 and G2 polymorphisms.
source: To evaluate the impact of these polymorphisms in driving resistance/susceptibility to T.b. gambiense infection, G1 and G2 polymorphisms were genotyped in 227 T.b. gambiense-infected individuals and 104 controls from the mangrove focus in Guinea.
evidence: This describes the study design and sample collection for the Guinea cohort.

claim: Neither G1 nor G2 variant demonstrated an association with susceptibility to T.b. gambiense infection (p=0.47 [G1], p=0.50 [G2]).
source: When compared to control genotype frequencies, neither variant demonstrated an association with susceptibility to T.b. gambiense infection (p=0.47 [G1], p=0.50 [G2], Table 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's statistical analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: T.b. gambiense-infected individuals can be subdivided into clinical stage trypanosomiasis patients (n = 167) and latent carriers (n = 60).
source: T.b. gambiense-infected individuals can be subdivided into clinical stage trypanosomiasis patients who are serology and microscopy positive for trypanosomiasis (n = 167), and latent carriers (n = 60), who are defined as strongly serology positive, but asymptomatic and aparasitemic by microscopic examination for a period of at least two years.
evidence: This describes the classification of study participants.

claim: Latent carriers are defined as strongly serology positive, but asymptomatic and aparasitemic by microscopic examination for a period of at least two years.
source: T.b. gambiense-infected individuals can be subdivided into clinical stage trypanosomiasis patients who are serology and microscopy positive for trypanosomiasis (n = 167), and latent carriers (n = 60), who are defined as strongly serology positive, but asymptomatic and aparasitemic by microscopic examination for a period of at least two years.
evidence: This describes the definition of latent carriers used in the study.

claim: Significant opposing associations were observed for the two APOL1 variants with T.b. gambiense infection outcome when comparing clinical cases and latent carriers.
source: When comparing clinical cases and latent carriers, significant opposing associations were observed for the two APOL1 variants with T.b. gambiense infection outcome (Table 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's statistical analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: The G1 variant associates with dominant protection against developing clinical stage trypanosomiasis (OR = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.17–0.62; p=0.0005).
source: There was an association between the G1 variant and dominant protection against developing clinical stage trypanosomiasis (OR = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.17–0.62; p=0.0005).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's statistical analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: T.b. gambiense-infected individuals possessing a copy of the G1 APOL1 variant were three-fold more likely to be latent asymptomatic carriers.
source: This indicates that T.b. gambiense-infected individuals possessing a copy of the G1 APOL1 variant were three-fold more likely to be latent asymptomatic carriers of T.b. gambiense.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the odds ratio from the statistical analysis.

claim: The G2 variant was associated with a three-fold increased susceptibility to clinical stage trypanosomiasis (OR = 3.08, 95% CI: 1.45–7.06, p=0.0025).
source: In contrast, the G2 variant was associated with a three-fold increased susceptibility to clinical stage trypanosomiasis (OR = 3.08, 95% CI: 1.45–7.06, p=0.0025), consistent with a risk of faster disease progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's statistical analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: The G2 association with clinical stage trypanosomiasis was strengthened (OR = 5.87, 95% CI: 2.16–20.01; p=0.0001) when individuals with a compound heterozygous (G1/G2) genotype were excluded.
source: This association was strengthened still further (OR = 5.87, 95% CI: 2.16–20.01; p=0.0001) when individuals with a potentially antagonistic compound heterozygous (G1/G2) genotype were excluded from the analysis (Table 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's statistical analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: The G1 and G2 APOL1 variants exhibit distinct subspecies-specific susceptibility profiles in relation to T.b. rhodesiense and T.b. gambiense.
source: Together these associations, summarised in Figure 2A, indicate that the G1 and G2 APOL1 variants exhibit distinct subspecies-specific susceptibility profiles in relation to the two causative agents of human African trypanosomiasis.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the study's findings, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The G1 variant is associated with asymptomatic carriage of T.b. gambiense, but the predicted protection against T.b. rhodesiense infection was not detected.
source: The G1 variant is associated with asymptomatic carriage of T.b. gambiense, but the predicted protection against T.b. rhodesiense infection (Genovese et al., 2010) was not detected.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings for G1.

claim: For the G2 variant, opposing dominant associations were observed with T.b. rhodesiense and T.b. gambiense.
source: For the G2 variant, opposing dominant associations were observed with the two different subspecies.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings for G2.

claim: The G2 association is protective against T.b. rhodesiense infection, but with increased susceptibility to a more severe disease outcome for T.b. gambiense.
source: This association is protective against T.b. rhodesiense infection, but with increased susceptibility to a more severe disease outcome for T.b. gambiense.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings for G2.

claim: Data generated by this study were merged with previously reported allele frequencies for 38 other sub-Saharan African populations, producing a cohort of 5287 genotyped samples.
source: To visualize the geographic distribution of APOL1 variants in relation to HAT endemicity (Figure 2B), data generated by this study were merged with previously reported allele frequencies for 38 other sub-Saharan African populations, to produce a cohort of 5287 genotyped samples.
evidence: This describes the methodology for creating the geographical distribution maps.

claim: Both G1 and G2 variants are reported at higher prevalence in T.b. gambiense endemic West Africa.
source: Both variants are reported at higher prevalence in T.b. gambiense endemic West Africa, particularly G1, which reaches frequencies as high as 49% in the Ibo (Thomson et al., 2014) and Esan (Abecasis et al., 2012) tribes of Nigeria, decreasing to complete absence in Northeast Africa (Tzur et al., 2010; Behar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies and illustrated in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: G1 reaches frequencies as high as 49% in the Ibo and Esan tribes of Nigeria.
source: Both variants are reported at higher prevalence in T.b. gambiense endemic West Africa, particularly G1, which reaches frequencies as high as 49% in the Ibo (Thomson et al., 2014) and Esan (Abecasis et al., 2012) tribes of Nigeria, decreasing to complete absence in Northeast Africa (Tzur et al., 2010; Behar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thomson et al., 2014 and Abecasis et al., 2012.

claim: G1 decreases to complete absence in Northeast Africa.
source: Both variants are reported at higher prevalence in T.b. gambiense endemic West Africa, particularly G1, which reaches frequencies as high as 49% in the Ibo (Thomson et al., 2014) and Esan (Abecasis et al., 2012) tribes of Nigeria, decreasing to complete absence in Northeast Africa (Tzur et al., 2010; Behar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tzur et al., 2010 and Behar et al., 2011.

claim: G1 allele frequency is moderately inversely correlated with longitude (Pearson correlation: r = −0.526, p=2.0 × 10−4, N = 40).
source: Allele frequency is moderately inversely correlated with longitude for both G1 (Pearson correlation: r = −0.526, p=2.0 × 10−4, N = 40) and G2 (r = −0.593, p=5.7 × 10−5, N = 37) but not latitude (G1, p=0.33, G2, p=0.30), indicating a significant decreasing relative frequency for both APOL1 variants from West to East across the continent.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of geographical distribution data.

claim: G2 allele frequency is moderately inversely correlated with longitude (r = −0.593, p=5.7 × 10−5, N = 37).
source: Allele frequency is moderately inversely correlated with longitude for both G1 (Pearson correlation: r = −0.526, p=2.0 × 10−4, N = 40) and G2 (r = −0.593, p=5.7 × 10−5, N = 37) but not latitude (G1, p=0.33, G2, p=0.30), indicating a significant decreasing relative frequency for both APOL1 variants from West to East across the continent.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of geographical distribution data.

claim: G1 and G2 allele frequencies are not correlated with latitude (G1, p=0.33, G2, p=0.30).
